item.title: Slim Thug Brings Houston’s Slabs & Small Businesses Back Together
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Slim Thug revives Houston's King of Cars festival with custom slabs, a marketplace for local brands and a hometown rap lineup.
item.content:encoded:
Slim Thug is bringing King of Cars back to Houston after nearly a decade, and he wants the city’s small businesses on the floor alongside the slabs.

The custom car show and culture festival returns Sunday, November 22, with a marketplace for local vendors and a lineup drawn from Houston rap.

In an interview with KPRC 2, the North Side rapper described the festival as a citywide flea market where people from different neighborhoods can show what they make.

He’s inviting fashion brands, entrepreneurs and creators to meet people who might not otherwise come across their work.

“I just wanted to do something where everybody can kind of show their brands, whatever they’re working on, and get the city to see it,” Slim Thug told KPRC 2.

The show runs from 1 to 8 P.M. in Halls D and E at Houston’s Reliant Center and in addition to Slim Thug, Paul Wall, Lil’ Keke, Z-Ro, Kirko Bangz, Lil Flip, DJ XO and Propain will also be present.

Slabs are the Houston customs best known for candy paint, loud sound systems and wire rims that stick out from the wheels, called swangas.

Slim Thug wants them next to imported sports cars and custom trucks, with room for people who build and drive different kinds of cars.

He got the idea to revive the show by looking back at “Still Tippin’,” the Mike Jones single that featured him and Paul Wall.

Its video put Houston’s cars and its rappers in the same frame, a choice director Dr. Teeth recalled to AllHipHop when he described shooting it in Houston for a street-level Swishahouse feel.

The 2004 single later appeared on Jones’ debut album, Who Is Mike Jones?

Slim Thug has kept showing his cars in Houston between King of Cars events.

At a Coffee and Cars meetup at Post Houston last November, more than a hundred people gathered in a downtown parking lot where his Rolls-Royce shared space with local slabs and cars that other attendees brought to show.

Families can also look for a designated children’s area and a gaming section where visitors can play Grand Theft Auto.

item.title: Swizz Beatz & Alicia Keys Bring Black Art And Dirt-Bike Culture To Baltimore
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Swizz Beatz and Alicia Keys bring roughly 130 works to Baltimore, including Amy Sherald's tribute to the city's dirt-bike riders.
item.content:encoded:
Swizz Beatz and Alicia Keys are bringing Amy Sherald’s paintings of Baltimore dirt-bike riders to the city that inspired them.

The works are part of a touring show the producer and singer built from the art they collected together.

The Baltimore Museum of Art announced that Giants will open there April 18, 2027, with about 130 works by Black artists.

The collection spans generations, from 18 Gordon Parks photographs of Black life and the civil rights movement to paintings by Jordan Casteel and Tschabalala Self.

One of the works coming to town is Amy Sherald’s Deliverance, a pair of paintings inspired by Baltimore’s dirt-bike culture.

Swizz told PBS News Hour in an interview that Sherald called him to her studio without telling him the piece was ready, then showed him two riders pulling wheelies.

He said the painter had a personal memory behind the work: “from living in Baltimore, she used to see the Ruff Ryders, which is my family’s company, ride bikes all through her block.”

Seeing the two bikes as he came around the corner nearly made him faint, he recalled.

The Baltimore lineup also includes Floater 74, a four-part work by Derrick Adams that puts Black leisure at the center.

Museum director Asma Naeem said, “many of the artists featured in Giants will be familiar to visitors who attended The Culture: Hip Hop and Contemporary Art in the 21st Century.”

Swizz traces his interest in art back to seeing graffiti on his way to and from school in the Bronx. He and Keys also bring those shared interests into their music, including the Lovers Rose project they built around lowrider soul.

The museum will use its Contemporary Wing and a second gallery in its center for prints, drawings and photographs.

That puts works across several media under one ticket, including Arthur Jafa’s eight-foot sculpture Big Wheel I and Titus Kaphar’s three-panel piece inspired by Muhammad Ali’s fight with Sonny Liston.

The Brooklyn Museum organized Giants and launched it in 2024.

Baltimore follows the show’s Indianapolis run at Newfields, which closes February 28, 2027, after earlier stops in cities including Atlanta, Minneapolis and Richmond.

The BMA will show the collection through August 8, 2027, with tickets and tour bookings available in spring.

item.title: Rockstar Licensed More Than 250 UMPG Songs For GTA VI
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: UMPG says GTA VI includes more than 250 of its licensed songs, with dozens written for the game and 13 tracks on the album.
item.content:encoded:
Grand Theft Auto VI features more than 250 songs licensed from Universal Music Publishing Group, the company said in a statement sent to AllHipHop.

That catalog spans nine decades and includes dozens of new compositions written specifically for Rockstar Games’ latest release.

“The release of Grand Theft Auto VI is simply one of the biggest cultural moments in entertainment, and I’m thrilled that UMPG songwriters play such an integral role in the experience Rockstar Games has created,” said Jody Gerson, chairman and CEO of Universal Music Publishing Group.

Gerson continued: “Our extensive presence in GTA VI reflects the singular talents of our songwriters, the depth of our incomparable catalog and the strength and dedication of our sync team, which collaborated closely with the studio for years on the game, its trailers and the soundtrack album. I deeply appreciate Rockstar’s recognition of the value of songs and songwriters and its understanding of music’s power to engage audiences around the world and draw them more deeply into the game’s storytelling and action.”

The publisher’s tally covers the game itself. The separate 34-track Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album includes 13 tracks with contributions from its writers. Metro Boomin appears on Yung Lean’s “That’s It” with Future and is credited on Young Thug’s “WAKIN UP.”

UMPG also represents SZA, who appears on Justice’s “Flower in a Hurricane.”

Rockstar used “Flower in a Hurricane” in the launch trailer. It was part of a rollout that put UMPG songs in each of four major trailers.

Mike Campbell co-wrote Tom Petty’s “Love Is a Long Road,” which backed the reveal in December 2023.

The second trailer used the Pointer Sisters’ “Hot Together,” written by Sharon Robinson.

UMPG cited Luminate figures showing the song drew nearly 9.6 million global on-demand audio streams in the eight weeks afterward. It had drawn nearly 300,000 in all of 2024.

The game reaches deeper into the publisher’s catalog than its trailers do. The collection includes Sister Rosetta Tharpe and Marie Knight’s 1947 recording of “Didn’t It Rain” and John Lee Hooker’s 1948 “Boogie Chillen.”

Rockstar released the game on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, adding new stations to a series that has long put artists behind the radio mic.

item.title: Spotify Hasn’t Tested AI Remixes With Users As It Waits On Artist Consent
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Spotify's CFO says its AI remix tool hasn't reached user testing and still needs enough artists to give their permission.
item.content:encoded:
Spotify has struck deals with music companies for its planned AI remix tool, but it still needs artists to say yes.

Chief Financial Officer Christian Luiga said at Morgan Stanley’s technology and media conference in Barcelona that the company thinks the product is ready. It hasn’t put the feature in listeners’ hands, and it wants enough artists to take part before it goes live.

“We haven’t tried this product on any of our users yet,” Luiga said.

Spotify has reached agreements with Universal Music Group, Believe and Kobalt, but, he said, “we also need that consent from the artist.” Luiga said labels were better placed to answer questions about getting artists on board.

Luiga said the company wants a starting catalog broad enough to give fans a reason to use the tool.

While the conference moderator raised speculation about a possible launch window, Luiga didn’t give one.

Spotify announced its first remix licensing agreements with Universal Music Group in May. The deal covered both recordings and publishing.

Under Spotify’s deal with Believe, independent artists and labels served by Believe and TuneCore first decide whether they want to hear about AI programs at all. Those who do still have a separate choice about the Spotify offer.

Fan-made covers and remixes would link back to the original track, and Spotify said plays would generate royalties for participating artists and rights holders.

Luiga said those plays would draw from the existing streaming royalty pool; he didn’t give a price for making a remix.

The question of who gets paid had already reached the studio.

So So Def founder Jermaine Dupri asked Spotify to cut artists in when it makes money from AI versions of their work.

His comments came before Luiga’s update, as Spotify was lining up licensing partners.

item.title: J.PERIOD Brings A One-Take Mixtape To New Orleans With Dawn Richard
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: J.PERIOD and Josh Kun reschedule their live mixtape finale for December 3 with Dawn Richard, Flagboy Giz, Pell and more.
item.content:encoded:
J.PERIOD and Josh Kun have a new date for their New Orleans show, and Dawn Richard, Flagboy Giz and Pell are on the bill.

The Art of the Crossfade will close out its four-city run on Thursday, December 3 at Music Box Village with a Hip-Hop mixtape made onstage in one take.

The date puts New Orleans back on the calendar after the Jazz Generations Initiative postponed the October 10 show because of expected severe weather.

The series had already visited Phoenix in September and went ahead with its Lincoln, Nebraska, stop in October. New Orleans now closes out the run.

Leyla McCalla, Raj Smoove, Yusa and Girls Play Trumpets Too join the lineup, according to the organizers.

The evening starts with a musical lecture and audience participation before turning the stage over to the musicians, DJs and other voices from New Orleans.

J.PERIOD and Kun took the idea behind the show to a TEDx audience in 2014, years before they brought it on the road.

Their starting point was the slider on a DJ mixer that lets one track fade into another, but they wanted to know what else you could bring together that way.

When the tour opened in Los Angeles in July, Grand Performances asked people to bring a song that told their own story.

J.PERIOD mixed those submissions on the spot and brought some of the songs and stories into the evening performance.

J.PERIOD has been making mixtapes in front of crowds long before this tour.

In 2010, he and Black Thought turned a Toronto festival set into a recording, with the Roots MC rapping over live remixes and doing impressions of some of his favorite rappers.

The New Orleans show is free and open to all ages, but you have to RSVP. Doors open at 6 P.M. and the show starts at 7.

Dawn Richard at a New Orleans event in July 2026 (file photo). Photo: Danielle G. Campbell, CC BY-SA 4.0. Cropped.

item.title: Sexyy Red Plays Herself & Joins Real Dimez On GTA VI Remix
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Sexyy Red turns up as herself in GTA VI and shares a remix credit with Real Dimez, the game's fictional Vice City rap duo.
item.content:encoded:
Sexyy Red plays herself in Grand Theft Auto VI, but her name isn’t just in the cast list. She also joins Real Dimez, a fictional rap duo in the game, on “Cooties (Remix).”

Rockstar Games’ credits list two versions of “Cooties,” and the original belongs to the duo alone. Sexyy Red has a writing credit on the remix. DJ Slugo, Cardo Got Wings, Yung Exclusive, Johnny Juliano and Bornbad! produced both versions.

Real Dimez are characters, but the women behind them are working rappers. Hood Brat plays Bae-Luxe and Krissy Celess plays Roxy Rashad. Both performers are listed as writers on the two versions of “Cooties.”

Rockstar introduces the pair with four words: “Viral videos. Viral hooks.” Bae-Luxe and Roxy have been friends since high school, and their first taste of success came with another local rapper, DWNPLY.

By the time the game picks up their story, they’ve signed with Only Raw Records and are trying to get another hit.

That earlier collaboration has a real recording behind it, too. Denzel Curry plays DWNPLY and teams with Real Dimez on “Bulletproof Ski Mask.” Cardo, Yung Exclusive and Johnny Juliano worked on that track as well as both versions of “Cooties.”

The game had already put Sexyy Red’s music in front of players before launch.

Rockstar’s extended gameplay preview used “Pound Town,” the breakout single she made with Tay Keith. Rockstar also credits her on “WHATCHU KNOW ABOUT ME” with GloRilla and includes “Hoochie Coochie” among its licensed songs. Players can tune in on foot or in a car.

The “Cooties” remix isn’t the only place the fictional duo got actual producers behind the boards.

Take A Daytrip produced Real Dimez’s “Money Don’t Lie.” ATL Jacob shares production credit with RushDee and Corey Dollaz on another track, “Vibin’ With The Dimez.”

Grand Theft Auto VI went on sale November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, with Vice City set in Rockstar’s fictional state of Leonida.

item.title: Wu-Tang Clan Reunites With Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith For Detroit’s Thanksgiving Halftime
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Wu-Tang Clan brings Chad Smith back into the fold, taking a studio pairing from 2000 to Detroit's Thanksgiving stage.
item.content:encoded:
Wu-Tang Clan is bringing back a drummer from one of its loudest studio detours.

The Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith will play with the group during the Detroit Lions’ Thanksgiving halftime show, the team announced on X.

Smith and Wu-Tang crossed paths on Loud Rocks, the 2000 compilation that paired rap acts with rock musicians.

He played drums on a new version of “Wu-Tang Clan Ain’t Nothing Ta F**K Wit,” with Rage Against the Machine’s Tom Morello on guitar and RZA, Inspectah Deck and Method Man on the mic.

The Lions named Smith as a guest but gave no set list or details about how much of the halftime show he’ll play.

Smith grew up in Bloomfield Hills and played Detroit clubs and bars before the Chili Peppers took him far beyond Michigan. He played Ford Field with Honolulu Boom, the Lions’ own drumline, at a playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams in January 2024.

Eminem and Paul Rosenberg are back for their second year as executive producers, with a hand in choosing the performers.

Last Thanksgiving, Eminem stepped out during Jack White’s set for “‘Till I Collapse.”

The producers picked Wu-Tang to headline this time, and the group enters Ford Field less than two weeks after its Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction.

Football isn’t the only reason Smith has been back behind a kit in Michigan lately.

He played with the University of Michigan’s marching band last year when he announced the Curtis & Joan Smith Scholarship, named for his parents. The scholarship offers need-based support for incoming music students.

CBS will carry the Chicago Bears-Detroit Lions game from Ford Field at 1 p.m. Eastern on November 26.

item.title: Issa Rae & Tracy Oliver’s Houston Drama “Open” Lands At HBO
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Issa Rae and Tracy Oliver bring an open-marriage drama to HBO, teaming up again after their early days making a web series.
item.content:encoded:
Issa Rae and Tracy Oliver have a home for the first drama they’ve written together. HBO landed Open for development, Deadline reports, bringing the two writers back together about 15 years after The Misadventures of Awkward Black Girl.

The new project follows a married couple in Houston who hope opening their marriage will keep them together. Their decision doesn’t stay between them. It sets off affairs and forces their friends to deal with secrets and problems of their own.

Oliver is set to run the show, and executive produce it with Rae, Jax Clark of Hoorae, E. Brian Dobbins, David Becky and Jonathan Berry. HBO and Paramount Television Studios are the studios behind the project, which came out of Rae’s first-look deal with Paramount Television Studios.

The drama drew seven offers after it went out to buyers in August. HBO, Paramount+ and Peacock made the final round, but Paramount+ was out of the running after its parent company and Warner Bros. Discovery merged in October. HBO ultimately beat Peacock for the project.

Rae and Oliver had a different starting point with Awkward Black Girl. Oliver produced the web series and played Rae’s co-worker Nina.

The series helped bring Rae to HBO, where Insecure ran for five seasons and earned 14 Emmy nominations.

Rae later created Rap Sh!t for HBO Max, which followed two women trying to build a rap career together in Miami. City Girls members Yung Miami and JT were co-executive producers.

In an interview with AllHipHop, Rae put it simply: “My favorite thing has to be the music. Like I love Shawna & Mia as a group. I love their chemistry.”

Raedio brought in outside artists for the soundtrack, too, with new material from Dreezy, Tokyo Jetz and Jean Deaux.

Oliver also created Harlem and co-wrote Girls Trip. There’s no premiere date or cast announced for Open, and picking up the project for development doesn’t mean HBO has ordered a season. Rae has a separate comedy pilot at the network with Insecure showrunner Prentice Penny.

Oliver is also developing Hilary, a Bel-Air spinoff centered on Coco Jones’ character, at Peacock.

item.title: Snoh Aalegra Gets Stevie Wonder’s Nod For Babyface & No I.D. Collaboration
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Snoh Aalegra explains how a pair of dates led to a Babyface co-write and why she wanted Stevie Wonder in the mix.
item.content:encoded:
Snoh Aalegra brought Babyface and No I.D. together on “Timeless,” then got Stevie Wonder’s approval to use a sample.

Her account of putting the record together starts with two dates she wanted to remember, not a list of names she wanted in the credits.

Aalegra said in an interview with Rolling Stone that she wrote the song with Babyface about the first two outings with the person behind much of Legendary Love.

She remembered him working on his guitar and helping her get the details of those encounters into the song. Aalegra described her excitement at hearing Babyface sing while they worked.

“I told No ID I wanted to have a Stevie Wonder sample in here,” Aalegra said. “I was so happy when Stevie approved,” Aalegra said.

The released song credits him and songwriter Yvonne Wright alongside Aalegra and Babyface.

The production credits list No I.D., Babyface and Josh Grant. Aalegra also described working with Raphael Saadiq as she developed the recording.

She already knew the Chicago producer’s way of working long before “Timeless.” In her first interview with AllHipHop, she recalled meeting No I.D. through family and eventually joining his ARTium roster after he heard the material she was making.

On her early ballad “You Always Knew,” Aalegra said No I.D. had her speak the words over the piano before easing back into melody.

She usually handled her own vocal production, but his approach showed her that a performance could change a song without rewriting it.

“He’s amazing at painting a picture, and he really wants to know what the song means and what I want to say with the song,” Sno Aalegra said.

That same studio circle put her on Common’s 2014 album Nobody’s Smiling on “Hustle Harder.” Common separately recorded a verse for her song “Bad Things” while she was visiting family in Sweden, after hearing the beat and her vocals in the studio.

No I.D. called her with the news. Aalegra told AllHipHop she preferred collaborations to start that way, with someone responding to a record rather than joining it as a favor.

Wonder’s music had already found its way into Aalegra’s writing before she asked to sample him. On “I Want You Around,” she named his album Innervisions, a reference she brought up while explaining how “Timeless” came together.

Legendary Love arrived November 13 with “Timeless” in the ninth slot of its 13-song sequence.

item.title: Big Boi Revisits The Two Rejections Before OutKast’s Christmas Breakthrough
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Big Boi looks back on how two early setbacks led OutKast to an unlikely opening on a LaFace Christmas compilation.
item.content:encoded:
Big Boi revisited the two times OutKast got passed over before the Atlanta duo landed a Christmas album slot and turned it into “Player’s Ball.”

The assignment wasn’t an obvious fit for two young rappers trying to get Atlanta heard.

The story came up on Big Boi’s Bloodlines & Basslines, in an episode about the setbacks that put him and his sons on different paths.

In an interview with Bullseye, Big Boi recalled finally getting a shot at a single, only to learn it was for a holiday compilation. “It was like they’re trying to end our career before it even started!” he said.

OutKast was passed over twice, and Big Boi and André 3000 had no intention of making a Christmas record that sounded like anybody else’s.

The first title was “Socks and Drawers.” Big Boi explained that instead of reaching for a Christmas story they didn’t recognize, the pair wrote about spending the day at the Dungeon, where making music was the main thing.

Sleepy Brown told GQ that Organized Noize producer Ray Murray had been working on the beat for Left Eye’s group when Rico Wade heard it. Big Boi remembered being given a choice between the beat that became their single and the one TLC used for “Sleigh Ride.” OutKast took the former.

Sleepy said Wade began sketching the scene in the studio, which gave him the idea for the hook. He told Bullseye that Curtis Mayfield’s falsetto helped him find the sound. LaFace later took out the sleigh bells and changed the holiday reference in the hook, Big Boi recalled, so the single could stay on the radio after Christmas.

The single topped the rap chart and helped carry Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik, OutKast’s 1994 debut, well past that first holiday. RCA dates the release to November 19, 1993, and still lists the Christmas mix.

Decades later, Big Boi started the podcast with his sons Bamboo and Cross, putting the story in a conversation about what people do after hearing no. He had turned down the idea of doing a podcast until he could make it a conversation with his kids.

OutKast entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2025.
